plan.chapterName: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, chapter 8: Advanced Theories of Covalent Bonding
plan.contextChunk: This figure sets three block diagrams side by side, each a schematic picture of the molecular orbital bands of a solid with energy increasing upward. Every diagram is built the same way: a lower blue-violet rectangle labeled Valence, an upper green rectangle labeled Conduction, and between them an empty white region whose left and right edges are marked by vertical dashed lines and which is spanned by a double-headed vertical arrow labeled Band gap. The leftmost diagram, headed Insulator, is drawn with the widest separation, its conduction block sitting far above the valence block. The middle diagram, headed Semiconductor, repeats the construction with a gap roughly half as tall, and the whole stack sits lower on the page. The rightmost diagram, headed Conductor, shows the two blocks almost touching, the gap reduced to a thin white sliver so narrow that its Band gap label has to be placed outside the diagram to the right. Since the three diagrams share identical block widths and colors, the only quantity that changes across the row is the height of the white region, which is what the reader is meant to measure by eye. The progression underlies the account of electrical conduction in solids, in which electrons must be promoted out of the filled valence band into the empty conduction band and the energy needed to do so is set by the separation between them.

interactionPlan.concept: In a solid, the energy separation between the filled valence band and the empty conduction band — the band gap — determines whether electrons can be promoted into mobile states, classifying the material as an insulator, semiconductor, or conductor.
elements: Three side-by-side band diagrams on a white background, all with identical block widths and colors, filling the full width of the frame
Panel headings in bold: 'Insulator', 'Semiconductor', 'Conductor', centered above each pair of blocks
Blue-violet filled rectangle labeled 'Valence' at the bottom of each panel (same width and height in all three)
Yellow-green filled rectangle labeled 'Conduction' above the valence block in each panel (same width and height in all three)
White empty gap region between the two blocks of each panel; its height is the only quantity that differs across panels
Short vertical dashed guide lines at the left and right edges of each white gap (vestigial in the conductor panel where the gap is a thin sliver)
Double-headed vertical arrow spanning each gap, labeled 'Band gap' in the insulator and semiconductor panels
Conductor panel: 'Band gap' written outside to the LEFT of the sliver with a short leader line, kept clear of any other annotation
Optional (hidden by default) faint vertical 'Energy' arrow with label along the far left edge
Optional (hidden by default) numeric gap value in eV beside each gap arrow, appearing only once the slider is engaged
Optional (hidden by default) small dark circles representing electrons at the top of each valence band
Optional (hidden by default) horizontal dotted marker line above the valence band top, labeled 'typical excitation energy (schematic)'
Optional (hidden by default) promotion arrow: solid green arrow reaching the conduction band on success, dashed grey arrow stalling inside the gap on failure
Optional (hidden by default) short result caption near the active panel: 'Electron promoted — current flows' or 'Gap too wide — no conduction'
Optional (hidden by default) compact legend: green = conduction band (empty), blue-violet = valence band (filled), white = forbidden gap
Live classification caption under the adjustable panel reading 'Conductor', 'Semiconductor', or 'Insulator' (shown only while the slider is engaged)

interactions.label: Band gap (eV)
interactions.teaches: At its default of 0 the slider is disengaged and the figure shows the textbook's three unlabeled qualitative gaps; dragging it turns on numeric eV values and morphs a single panel continuously, showing that conductor, semiconductor and insulator are one picture with one varying distance.
interactions.default_behavior: Value 0 means 'not engaged' — no eV numbers, no adjustable panel, source figure only.

interactions.teaches: Clicking a panel reveals its valence electrons and launches one upward with a fixed packet of excitation energy; it reaches the conduction band only when the gap is narrower than that packet, so a wide gap physically blocks conduction.

interactions.label: Excitation energy supplied
interactions.teaches: Raising the supplied energy raises the schematic marker line, so a semiconductor that could not be crossed before now can — semiconductor conductivity rises with temperature, while the insulator's gap remains far too wide.

demo_steps.title: The figure as printed
demo_steps.narration: Three materials, one picture: identical filled valence bands and identical empty conduction bands, with only the height of the white forbidden gap changing from left to right. No axis, no numbers — just the qualitative comparison.

demo_steps.title: Try to promote an electron
demo_steps.narration: Click the insulator panel. Electrons appear at the top of the valence band and one is pushed upward, but the arrow stalls inside the forbidden gap — the supplied energy marker sits far below the conduction band, so no current flows.

demo_steps.title: Supply more energy
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the higher excitation energy and click the semiconductor. The marker now rises above its narrow gap and the arrow turns solid green into the conduction band — semiconductors conduct better as they are heated or illuminated.

demo_steps.title: Put a number on the gap
demo_steps.narration: Engaging the slider adds an energy axis and eV values and turns one panel adjustable. At about 4 eV the conduction band sits far above the valence band and the caption reads Insulator.

demo_steps.title: Shrink toward a semiconductor
demo_steps.narration: Bring the conduction band down to roughly 1 eV. The label switches to Semiconductor: the gap is now comparable to energies electrons can realistically pick up from heat or light.

demo_steps.title: Close the gap: a conductor
demo_steps.narration: Slide the bands almost together. The white region becomes a sliver, electrons enter empty conduction states at essentially no energy cost, and the material is a conductor.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Insulators, semiconductors and conductors are not three different diagrams — they are the same diagram with one distance changed: how much energy an electron must gain to leave the filled valence band and reach the empty conduction band.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Layout: three block-pairs left to right (Insulator, Semiconductor, Conductor) on white, sized so the drawing fills the container edge to edge with only small margins — tighten the viewBox so no dead space remains below the diagram. All body text at least 12 px effective size; 'Conduction', 'Valence' and 'Band gap' should be clearly larger than the surrounding chrome and centered on their blocks. Colors: muted blue-violet 'Valence' rectangle at bottom, yellow-green 'Conduction' rectangle above, white forbidden gap between, thin dark outlines. Insulator has the tallest white gap with dashed edge guides and a long black double-headed 'Band gap' arrow; semiconductor repeats this at roughly half the height; conductor shows only a thin sliver with 'Band gap' written outside to the LEFT on a short leader line, well separated from any dotted energy-marker text on the right. STEP-0 DEFAULT MUST MATCH THE TEXTBOOK: no energy axis, no eV numbers, no legend, no electron dots, no excitation-energy line, no classification caption — these appear only after a click, a toggle change, or a nonzero slider value. When revealed, the horizontal marker is a neutral grey/blue dotted line labeled 'typical excitation energy (schematic)' with no asserted numeric value at a stated temperature; avoid any claim like '0.70 eV at 300 K'. Promotion arrow is solid green when it reaches the conduction band, dashed grey when it stalls in the gap, with a short one-line caption beside it. When the slider is engaged, add a faint upward 'Energy' arrow at the far left, eV values beside each gap arrow, and a bold caption under the adjustable panel: Conductor (<0.1 eV), Semiconductor (~0.1–3 eV), Insulator (>3 eV). Legend, if shown, sits compactly at the bottom with no trailing whitespace.

authoredContext:
In a solid, similar things happen, but on a much larger scale. Remember that even in a small sample there are a huge number of atoms (typically > 1023 atoms), and therefore a huge number of atomic orbitals that may be combined into molecular orbitals. When N valence atomic orbitals, all of the same energy and each containing one (1) electron, are combined, N/2 (filled) bonding orbitals and N/2 (empty) antibonding orbitals will result. Each bonding orbital will show an energy lowering as the atomic orbitals are mostly in-phase, but each of the bonding orbitals will be a little different and have slightly different energies. The antibonding orbitals will show an increase in energy as the atomic orbitals are mostly out-of-phase, but each of the antibonding orbitals will also be a little different and have slightly different energies. The allowed energy levels for all the bonding orbitals are so close together that they form a band, called the valence band. Likewise, all the antibonding orbitals are very close together and form a band, called the conduction band. The figure shows the bands for three important classes of materials: insulators, semiconductors, and conductors.

Molecular orbitals in solids are so closely spaced that they are described as bands. The valence band is lower in energy and the conduction band is higher in energy. The type of solid is determined by the size of the “band gap” between the valence and conduction bands. Only a very small amount of energy is required to move electrons from the valence band to the conduction band in a conductor, and so they conduct electricity well. In an insulator, the band gap is large, so that very few electrons move, and they are poor conductors of electricity. Semiconductors are in between: they conduct electricity better than insulators, but not as well as conductors.

This figure shows three diagrams. The first is labeled, “Insulator,” and it consists of two boxes. The “conduction” box is above and the “valence” box is below. A large gap marked by 4 dashed lines contains a double-headed arrow. One head pointing towards the “conduction box” and the other towards the “valence” box. The arrow is labeled, “Band gap.” The second diagram is similar to the first, but the band gap is about half as large. This diagram is labeled, “Semiconductor.” The third diagram is similar to the other two, but the band gap is about a fifth that of the “Semiconductor” diagram. This diagram is labeled, “Conductor.”

In order to conduct electricity, electrons must move from the filled valence band to the empty conduction band where they can move throughout the solid. The size of the band gap, or the energy difference between the top of the valence band and the bottom of the conduction band, determines how easy it is to move electrons between the bands. Only a small amount of energy is required in a conductor because the band gap is very small. This small energy difference is “easy” to overcome, so they are good conductors of electricity. In an insulator, the band gap is so “large” that very few electrons move into the conduction band; as a result, insulators are poor conductors of electricity. Semiconductors conduct electricity when “moderate” amounts of energy are provided to move electrons out of the valence band and into the conduction band. Semiconductors, such as silicon, are found in many electronics.

plan.concept: In a solid, the energy separation between the filled valence band and the empty conduction band — the band gap — determines whether electrons can be promoted into mobile states, classifying the material as a conductor, semiconductor, or insulator.
elements: Three side-by-side band diagrams sharing an implicit vertical energy axis (energy increases upward), with a faint 'Energy →' arrow and label along the left edge
Panel 1 heading: 'Insulator' (bold, centered above its blocks)
Panel 2 heading: 'Semiconductor' (bold, centered above its blocks)
Panel 3 heading: 'Conductor' (bold, centered above its blocks)
Blue-violet filled rectangle labeled 'Valence' at the bottom of each panel (identical width and height in all three)
Green filled rectangle labeled 'Conduction' above the valence block in each panel (identical width and height in all three)
White empty gap region between the two blocks in each panel, its height the only quantity that differs across panels
Vertical dashed lines marking the left and right edges of each white gap region (omitted or vestigial in the conductor panel where the gap is a thin sliver)
Double-headed vertical arrow spanning each gap, labeled 'Band gap'; in the conductor panel the label sits outside the diagram to the right with a short leader line
Numeric gap value annotation (in eV) beside each panel's gap arrow

Interactive fourth 'adjustable' panel (or highlighted active panel) whose conduction band moves vertically with the slider, with a live classification caption reading 'Conductor / Semiconductor / Insulator'
Small filled circles representing electrons sitting at the top of each valence band

Promotion arrow: an upward arrow from a valence electron toward the conduction band, drawn as a solid arrow that reaches the conduction band when promotion succeeds and a dashed, truncated arrow that stalls in the gap when it fails
Thermal-energy marker: a horizontal dotted line (and 'available energy, ~kT / thermal excitation' label) drawn a fixed height above the valence band top, compared against each gap height
Result callout text near the clicked panel: 'Electron promoted — current flows' or 'Not enough energy — no conduction'
Legend mapping green = conduction band (empty), blue-violet = valence band (filled), white = forbidden gap

interactions.label: Band gap (eV)
interactions.teaches: The conduction band slides up or down relative to the fixed valence band, and the material's name changes with it — conductor, semiconductor, insulator are not three different pictures but one picture with one varying distance.

Clicking a panel launches an electron upward with a fixed packet of available energy; it reaches the conduction band only when the gap is smaller than that energy, so a large gap physically blocks conduction.

interactions.label: Available thermal energy
interactions.teaches: Raising the temperature raises the energy marker, so a semiconductor that could not conduct now can — conductivity of semiconductors increases with temperature, while an insulator's gap is still far too wide.

demo_steps.title: One diagram, three materials
demo_steps.narration: All three panels use the same filled valence band and the same empty conduction band; only the white gap between them changes height. That single distance is the whole classification.

demo_steps.title: Widen the gap: an insulator
demo_steps.narration: Drag the conduction band far above the valence band. With a gap of several electron-volts, the label reads Insulator — electrons have nowhere accessible to go.

demo_steps.title: Try to promote an electron
demo_steps.narration: Click the panel. The promotion arrow rises only as far as the available-energy line and stalls inside the forbidden gap: no electron reaches the conduction band, so no current flows.

demo_steps.title: Shrink to a semiconductor
demo_steps.narration: Bring the conduction band down to about 1 eV above the valence band. The label switches to Semiconductor: the gap is now comparable to the energy a few electrons can pick up.

demo_steps.title: Heat the semiconductor
demo_steps.narration: Raise the thermal energy marker. The same 1 eV gap that mostly blocked promotion at room temperature is now crossed — semiconductor conductivity rises with temperature.

demo_steps.title: Close the gap: a conductor
demo_steps.narration: Slide the bands almost together. The white region becomes a sliver, electrons flow into empty conduction states with essentially no energy cost, and the material is a conductor.

plan.keyInsight: Conductors, semiconductors, and insulators are not different kinds of diagrams — they are the same diagram with one distance changed: how much energy an electron must gain to leave the filled valence band and enter the empty conduction band.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Three vertically stacked block pairs arranged left to right on a white background, all sharing identical block widths and colors: a muted blue-violet rectangle labeled 'Valence' on the bottom and a yellow-green rectangle labeled 'Conduction' above it, both with black centered sans-serif labels. Energy increases upward; the three panels are staggered so each valence block sits progressively lower/higher as in the original, emphasizing that only the white gap height differs. Left panel (Insulator) has the tallest white gap with tall vertical dashed lines on both edges and a long black double-headed arrow labeled 'Band gap' in its middle; middle panel (Semiconductor) repeats this with roughly half the gap height; right panel (Conductor) has only a thin white sliver, no room for an internal arrow, so 'Band gap' is written outside to the right. Bold black headings sit above each panel. Add small dark electron dots along the top edge of each valence band, a dotted horizontal 'available thermal energy' line drawn at a fixed height above the valence band top, and an animated promotion arrow that is solid green when it reaches the conduction band and dashed red-grey when it stalls inside the gap. Show the live gap value in eV next to each arrow and a bold classification caption under the adjustable panel that reads Conductor (<0.1 eV), Semiconductor (~0.1–3 eV), or Insulator (>3 eV).

discrepancies: Extra annotation layer not in the source clutters the figure: a faint vertical 'Energy' axis, a red dashed 'available energy' line running across all three panels, five electron dots drawn on each valence band, and a three-item legend — none of these appear in the original three-panel diagram.

Numeric eV values (5.50 / 1.10 / 0.05 eV) are appended under every 'Band gap' label; the source figure carries no numbers, and the 0.70 eV / 1.40 eV 'available energy at 300 K / 600 K' values are physically inflated (kT ≈ 0.026 eV at 300 K).

Overall text is rendered very small at inline size (980×500 viewBox squeezed into ~600 px): 'Conduction'/'Valence'/'Band gap' read far smaller relative to the blocks than in the source, and the 10.5 px red 'available energy ≈0.70 eV (300 K)' caption is effectively illegible.

Panel proportions differ: the generated blocks are narrower and shorter relative to the gaps, and the vertical scale is compressed as √E, so the insulator gap no longer looks proportionally as dominant as in the source; the conductor 'Band gap' leader label crowds the red energy-line caption.
The generated figure sits in the upper-left of the canvas with a large empty band of whitespace below the legend, unlike the tightly cropped source composition.
evaluation.notes: Structurally faithful three-panel band-gap diagram with correct colors, dashed gap edges, double-headed arrows and rich, genuinely functional interactions (slider, heat toggle, promotion animation, 6-step demo), but the added axis/legend/electron/available-energy layer clutters it and most text renders too small to read comfortably at inline size, with the 300 K 'available energy' value physically overstated.
action_items: Shrink the viewBox (or enlarge the panel layout) so the diagram fills the container and all body text renders at ≥12 px effective size; bump 'Conduction'/'Valence'/'Band gap' font sizes and drop the 10.5 px red caption to a legible size or move it into a tooltip.

Reduce non-source chrome in the default (step-0) state: hide the energy axis, legend, electron dots and red available-energy line until the user advances the demo or triggers a promotion, so step 0 reads as a drop-in replacement for the static figure.
Reposition the conductor 'Band gap' leader label so it does not crowd the red energy-line text, and remove the extra whitespace below the legend by tightening the vertical extent.
Correct or reframe the 'available energy' numbers (kT ≈ 0.026 eV at 300 K) — e.g. label the line as a schematic 'typical excitation energy' rather than asserting 0.70 eV at 300 K.

attempts.html:
Band gaps: one diagram, three materials Unchecked = Low (cool). The marker is schematic, not a measured value. Tip: hover or click any band or gap in the figure.
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: The whole diagram occupies only the upper-left ~60% of the canvas: the 620×252 viewbox leaves a large empty white band below the panels, so the figure reads smaller and less centered than the source's full-width three-panel layout.

Block proportions are slightly compressed relative to the source — in the original the conduction blocks are noticeably taller (roughly equal to or larger than the valence blocks) and the insulator gap is ~2.2× the semiconductor gap; here conduction blocks are squat and the gap ratio is ~1.9×.
The conductor panel adds a small leader tick from the block edge to the 'Band gap' text; the source has the label floating free beside the sliver (cosmetic only).

Non-default steps introduce elements absent from the source (energy axis, electron dots, 'typical excitation energy' dashed marker, eV numerals, classification captions) — acceptable as pedagogy, but they go well beyond the printed figure.
evaluation.notes: Default state is a clean, recognizable reproduction of the three-panel band-gap figure with correct colors, dashed gap guides and double-headed arrows, backed by genuinely useful slider/toggle/button/demo-step interactions; main weaknesses are the shrunken layout with large empty canvas below and slightly compressed block/gap proportions versus the source.
action_items: Enlarge the drawing within the viewbox (or shrink the viewbox height) so the three panels fill the container vertically and horizontally, matching the source's full-width composition.

plan.concept: In a solid, the energy separation between the filled valence band and the empty conduction band — the band gap — determines whether electrons can be promoted into mobile states, classifying the material as an insulator, semiconductor, or conductor.
elements: Three side-by-side band diagrams on a white background, all with identical block widths and colors, filling the full width of the frame
Panel headings in bold: 'Insulator', 'Semiconductor', 'Conductor', centered above each pair of blocks
Blue-violet filled rectangle labeled 'Valence' at the bottom of each panel (same width and height in all three)
Yellow-green filled rectangle labeled 'Conduction' above the valence block in each panel (same width and height in all three)
White empty gap region between the two blocks of each panel; its height is the only quantity that differs across panels
Short vertical dashed guide lines at the left and right edges of each white gap (vestigial in the conductor panel where the gap is a thin sliver)
Double-headed vertical arrow spanning each gap, labeled 'Band gap' in the insulator and semiconductor panels
Conductor panel: 'Band gap' written outside to the LEFT of the sliver with a short leader line, kept clear of any other annotation
Optional (hidden by default) faint vertical 'Energy' arrow with label along the far left edge
Optional (hidden by default) numeric gap value in eV beside each gap arrow, appearing only once the slider is engaged
Optional (hidden by default) small dark circles representing electrons at the top of each valence band
Optional (hidden by default) horizontal dotted marker line above the valence band top, labeled 'typical excitation energy (schematic)'
Optional (hidden by default) promotion arrow: solid green arrow reaching the conduction band on success, dashed grey arrow stalling inside the gap on failure
Optional (hidden by default) short result caption near the active panel: 'Electron promoted — current flows' or 'Gap too wide — no conduction'
Optional (hidden by default) compact legend: green = conduction band (empty), blue-violet = valence band (filled), white = forbidden gap
Live classification caption under the adjustable panel reading 'Conductor', 'Semiconductor', or 'Insulator' (shown only while the slider is engaged)

interactions.label: Band gap (eV)
interactions.teaches: At its default of 0 the slider is disengaged and the figure shows the textbook's three unlabeled qualitative gaps; dragging it turns on numeric eV values and morphs a single panel continuously, showing that conductor, semiconductor and insulator are one picture with one varying distance.
interactions.default_behavior: Value 0 means 'not engaged' — no eV numbers, no adjustable panel, source figure only.

interactions.teaches: Clicking a panel reveals its valence electrons and launches one upward with a fixed packet of excitation energy; it reaches the conduction band only when the gap is narrower than that packet, so a wide gap physically blocks conduction.

interactions.label: Excitation energy supplied
interactions.teaches: Raising the supplied energy raises the schematic marker line, so a semiconductor that could not be crossed before now can — semiconductor conductivity rises with temperature, while the insulator's gap remains far too wide.

demo_steps.title: The figure as printed
demo_steps.narration: Three materials, one picture: identical filled valence bands and identical empty conduction bands, with only the height of the white forbidden gap changing from left to right. No axis, no numbers — just the qualitative comparison.

demo_steps.title: Try to promote an electron
demo_steps.narration: Click the insulator panel. Electrons appear at the top of the valence band and one is pushed upward, but the arrow stalls inside the forbidden gap — the supplied energy marker sits far below the conduction band, so no current flows.

demo_steps.title: Supply more energy
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the higher excitation energy and click the semiconductor. The marker now rises above its narrow gap and the arrow turns solid green into the conduction band — semiconductors conduct better as they are heated or illuminated.

demo_steps.title: Put a number on the gap
demo_steps.narration: Engaging the slider adds an energy axis and eV values and turns one panel adjustable. At about 4 eV the conduction band sits far above the valence band and the caption reads Insulator.

demo_steps.title: Shrink toward a semiconductor
demo_steps.narration: Bring the conduction band down to roughly 1 eV. The label switches to Semiconductor: the gap is now comparable to energies electrons can realistically pick up from heat or light.

demo_steps.title: Close the gap: a conductor
demo_steps.narration: Slide the bands almost together. The white region becomes a sliver, electrons enter empty conduction states at essentially no energy cost, and the material is a conductor.

plan.keyInsight: Insulators, semiconductors and conductors are not three different diagrams — they are the same diagram with one distance changed: how much energy an electron must gain to leave the filled valence band and reach the empty conduction band.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Layout: three block-pairs left to right (Insulator, Semiconductor, Conductor) on white, sized so the drawing fills the container edge to edge with only small margins — tighten the viewBox so no dead space remains below the diagram. All body text at least 12 px effective size; 'Conduction', 'Valence' and 'Band gap' should be clearly larger than the surrounding chrome and centered on their blocks. Colors: muted blue-violet 'Valence' rectangle at bottom, yellow-green 'Conduction' rectangle above, white forbidden gap between, thin dark outlines. Insulator has the tallest white gap with dashed edge guides and a long black double-headed 'Band gap' arrow; semiconductor repeats this at roughly half the height; conductor shows only a thin sliver with 'Band gap' written outside to the LEFT on a short leader line, well separated from any dotted energy-marker text on the right. STEP-0 DEFAULT MUST MATCH THE TEXTBOOK: no energy axis, no eV numbers, no legend, no electron dots, no excitation-energy line, no classification caption — these appear only after a click, a toggle change, or a nonzero slider value. When revealed, the horizontal marker is a neutral grey/blue dotted line labeled 'typical excitation energy (schematic)' with no asserted numeric value at a stated temperature; avoid any claim like '0.70 eV at 300 K'. Promotion arrow is solid green when it reaches the conduction band, dashed grey when it stalls in the gap, with a short one-line caption beside it. When the slider is engaged, add a faint upward 'Energy' arrow at the far left, eV values beside each gap arrow, and a bold caption under the adjustable panel: Conductor (<0.1 eV), Semiconductor (~0.1–3 eV), Insulator (>3 eV). Legend, if shown, sits compactly at the bottom with no trailing whitespace.

discrepancies: In the source, the three valence bands sit on a common baseline and the conduction blocks rise progressively lower; the generated figure reproduces this, but the panel widths/heights are noticeably narrower relative to the source's wide blocks, and the overall figure occupies only the left third of the frame, leaving a large empty region below and right.

Source 'Band gap' text for insulator/semiconductor is centered beside the arrow at roughly the arrow midpoint with generous type size; in the generated figure the labels are small relative to the blocks and the semiconductor 'Band gap' text overlaps/abuts the dashed right guide line.

Source dashed guide lines for the insulator extend the full gap height at both block edges and are clearly visible; the generated version matches but uses thinner, lighter dashes that read faintly at inline size.

Conductor panel in the source has a very thin white sliver between the two bands with 'Band gap' text outside to the right; the generated version shows essentially no visible sliver, so the gap being labeled is not perceptible.
Text sizes overall are small relative to the block area compared to the source, where 'Conduction'/'Valence' nearly fill the block width.
evaluation.notes: A faithful, well-composed reproduction of the three-panel band-gap diagram with an excellent set of meaningful interactions (gap slider with live reclassification, excitation-energy toggle, promotion animation, 6-step demo); main weaknesses are small type relative to the blocks, an imperceptible conductor sliver, and a lot of unused canvas area.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are sound; remaining issues are purely implementation details (scale blocks to fill canvas, enlarge type, widen the conductor sliver, strengthen dashed guides and reposition overlapping labels).
